problems.description: The rewrite silently dropped the seed's authentication layer (JWT Bearer tokens, require_auth decorator, role-based users). The new SOAP operations are unauthenticated — an API that previously enforced auth now exposes write operations to anyone.

Wholesale rewrite discarded the existing modular architecture (Blueprints, JSON responses, token-based auth) in favor of a monolithic flat-function app.py with hand-rolled SOAP envelope/fault serialization via xml.etree — a non-idiomatic transport for a Flask API that reimplements what Flask-RESTful/marshmallow provide.

Cognitive complexity increased by +17 (SonarQube delta), concentrated in the custom XML parsing/serialization helpers (parse_operation, soap_fault, soap_response), which must be maintained by hand instead of a serialization framework.

9 convention violations (convention score 0.67): PascalCase and UPPER_CASE naming rules broken in app.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py, and test_app.py — inconsistent with the project's snake_case/PascalCase conventions.

New modules (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py) appear in a greenfield session with no evidence of wiring into the app entrypoint or tests, suggesting speculative infrastructure relative to the SOAP task API being delivered.

strengths: Smells decreased by -3 with zero new bugs and 0.0% duplication (SonarQube deltas).
Properly uses current_app.config and a current_app.config['DATABASE'] reference, enabling testability via config injection rather than a module-global constant.
Namespaced SOAP XML handling (ET.register_namespace, local_name/child_text helpers) is tidy and consistent, and the code is split into separate modules rather than one monolith.
Input validation exists for the create path (title required, strip/empty check) with proper SOAP fault responses.
commit_reviews.summary: The agent delivered working task-management functionality but regressed the seed's security posture and modular patterns by replacing Blueprint/JSON/JWT architecture with an unauthenticated hand-rolled SOAP stack, outweighed by the -3 smell reduction.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET_KEY falls back to the hardcoded 'development-only-secret' when the env var is unset, so any deployment that omits the env var ships with forgeable tokens.
Adds JSON/REST /auth/register and /auth/login endpoints to a SOAP XML service, mixing two API paradigms in one app rather than exposing auth through the existing SOAP envelope.
Zero test files changed despite +17 new functions (token_required, register, login, DB migration logic) — the auth feature has no automated coverage.
Migration backfills legacy rows to an auto-generated '__legacy__' user with an unreachable random credential, preserving data but permanently orphaning it from any real account.
New code relies on g.user_id being set by token_required, creating an implicit contract across handlers; +2 smells and cognitive complexity +28 support the coupling concern.
register returns 409 on duplicate username, allowing username enumeration; acceptable for a dev story but worth a uniform 400.

strengths: Owner scoping applied to every read/write path (create, list, get, update) — real defense-in-depth, not just auth-gate-only.
ALTER TABLE migration with legacy-row backfill keeps pre-existing data intact.
Reuses existing get_db/init_db/from_mapping patterns and the g-object idiom instead of inventing new plumbing.
Generic token_required decorator with correct bearer parsing and consistent 401 semantics.
Standard, secure primitives: werkzeug password hashing, JWT HS256, parameterized queries.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, security-improving feature that fits the existing Flask/SQLite structure, but the mechanical convention score of 0.67 is a repo-wide artifact — all listed violations except the pre-existing app.py one are in files this commit never touched (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py), so the diff itself adheres to conventions.

problems.description: The 'status -> completed' transition predicate is duplicated across SOAP update_task and the new REST update_task_rest; queue_completion_notification is extracted, but the transition check itself lives in two places and could drift.
The notification address is users.username aliased as owner_email, so a notification is sent to a login name rather than a real email address — a semantic mismatch in the data model.
Notification behavior is only tested on the new REST endpoint; the identical logic added to the SOAP update_task path is untested.
send_notification_email logs via print() instead of the app logger, inconsistent with the app's logging usage.
Celery + Redis broker is heavy infrastructure for a single email notification, though it matches the project's stated story-agent pattern of Flask/Celery apps on Redis 6379.

strengths: Transition-gated notification: only queues on an actual status change to 'completed', with a test covering the idempotent re-transition case.
Handlers decoupled from Celery via the extracted queue_completion_notification helper.
Tests mock send_notification_email.delay, so unit tests run without a live broker.
New REST endpoint reuses existing auth (token_required) and get_db patterns, and field names are whitelisted against SQL injection.
Celery app/config split into celery_config.py + notification_tasks.py with explicit task routing to a notifications queue.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-factored, well-tested additive feature that fits the codebase and reuses existing patterns, but introduces minor debt via duplicated transition logic, a username-as-email mismatch, and heavy Celery/Redis infrastructure.

problems.description: New repositories.py violates the module-level-constants UPPER_CASE rule (measured convention violation); this is the one violation introduced by this commit — the other 7 flagged files (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, test_app.py, app.py) are pre-existing and untouched here.

init_db() forwards auto-generated legacy credentials (username + password hash) into TaskRepository.initialize(), burying schema migration and backfill logic inside a repository method rather than a dedicated migration path — couples persistence with data migration.

get_task_repository()/get_user_repository() construct a fresh repository per handler call instead of caching per request via Flask's g; harmless today (connection is opened per repository method either way, no regression) but a missed per-request caching pattern.
soap_response() dispatches on isinstance(tasks, dict) to distinguish a single task from a list — a type-check polymorphism that is brittle if a repository ever returns a non-dict row type.

strengths: Extracts data access into TaskRepository/UserRepository, removing the duplicated SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE SQL repeated across every handler.
Decouples the app from the DB driver: soap_response no longer depends on sqlite3.Row, and sqlite3.IntegrityError leaks are replaced with a domain-level DuplicateRecordError mapped to 409.
update_task's dynamic SQL (string-joined placeholders) is replaced with a cleaner updates-dict that the repository translates.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive refactor that cleanly separates persistence into a repository layer and deduplicates SQL, introducing only one minor convention violation in the new file plus a small migration/backfill coupling inside initialize().

problems.description: rate_limit_key() re-implements the JWT decoding already done in token_required() (same secret, same HS256, same int(payload['sub'])). Two copies of the auth-parse logic can diverge; extracting a shared decode helper would remove the risk.
paginate_for_owner() runs SELECT COUNT(*) on every page, making each request O(n) over the owner's task rows; acceptable for this SQLite scale but not scalable to large tables.
Measured cognitive complexity +21 (SonarQube) is concentrated in the two new validation-heavy functions; readable but at the high end of the threshold.

The measured convention score (0.67, 9 violations) is dominated by pre-existing violations in files this commit did NOT touch (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py) plus worktree-wide heuristics; the diff itself introduces no new violations (all new functions snake_case, Limiter PascalCase, config keys UPPER_CASE).

New GET /tasks orders by id DESC while existing list_for_owner() orders by created_at DESC, id DESC; functionally equivalent given monotonic autoincrement ids, but the two endpoints state different orderings.

strengths: Per-user rate limiting keyed off the JWT sub with IP fallback, applied via default_limits to every endpoint including /auth/* — a real brute-force mitigation.
Limiter created per-app inside create_app() with a memory:// fallback when app.testing and no explicit storage URI, keeping the test suite hermetic and Redis-independent.
Cursor pagination is well-validated (positive ints, limit capped to 100, combined 400s) and returns a consistent {data, next_cursor, total} shape.
paginate_for_owner() follows the BaseRepository conventions exactly: connection() context manager, _as_dict(), parameterized SQL with cursor as an AND id < ? clause.
Comprehensive test coverage: multi-page cursor traversal, default/cap behavior, invalid-parameter 400s, and 429 with Retry-After on both authenticated and auth endpoints.
Dependency Flask-Limiter[redis]>=3.8,<4 pinned in the same style as existing requirements; SonarQube reports 0 new bugs and 0 new smells.
commit_reviews.summary: Session 5 cleanly layers per-user rate limiting and cursor pagination onto the existing app-factory/repository architecture with thorough tests and 0 new bugs or smells; the 0.67 convention score is a worktree-level artifact of pre-existing violations in files this commit never touched, while the diff itself is convention-clean.

compounding_issues: Notification 'email' is actually the username — Session 2's users schema never added an email column, and Session 3 reused username as the delivery address, a semantic mismatch that persists to the end.
Completed-transition notification logic is duplicated in both the SOAP update_task and REST update_task_rest paths (app.py:208 and app.py:320), two parallel surfaces that can drift.
Session 1 discarded the entire unrelated auth-api seed rather than reusing any of it; later sessions then preserved their own code strictly, so the seed's value was entirely foregone.
key_decisions: Session 1: honor the hard SOAP constraint with a single /soap endpoint (CreateTask/ListTasks/GetTask/UpdateTask + SOAP faults), defining the protocol shape every later session extends.
Session 2: add JWT bearer auth with owner-scoped task queries and a data-safe migration of pre-existing rows to a non-login legacy owner, establishing the multi-tenant boundary.
Session 3: introduce Celery async notifications fired only on a real transition into 'completed', plus REST PUT parity — the app's first async integration seam.
Session 4: extract a repository layer (abstract BaseRepository + UserRepository/TaskRepository) to remove all route-level SQLite access, stabilizing the data layer for Session 5.
Session 5: add cursor pagination (paginate_for_owner) and JWT-subject-aware rate limiting as cross-cutting hardening built directly on Sessions 2 and 4.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the arc. Session 1 was a clean greenfield rewrite of an unrelated seed into a focused SOAP API; Sessions 2 and 3 layered authentication/ownership and async notifications while preserving existing behavior; Session 4 paid down structural debt by extracting a repository layer; and Session 5 added cross-cutting pagination and rate limiting. Organization matured from a single monolith to a modular app/repository split, and the test suite grew in lockstep with each feature (27 tests covering ownership isolation, migration, notification transitions, pagination edge cases, and rate limits), all passing at the end.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, well-paced story where each session built deliberately on the prior ones — from a SOAP greenfield API through auth, async notifications, a repository refactor, and final hardening — with quality and test coverage improving consistently across all five sessions.
